T7A01: Sensitivity is a receiver's ability to detect weak signals. A more sensitive receiver can hear fainter signals.
T7A02: A transceiver combines a receiver and a transmitter in one unit, sharing circuits such as the frequency control. Most modern ham radios are transceivers.
T7A03: A mixer combines two signals to produce new frequencies (sum and difference). It's used to convert a signal from one frequency to another, as in a superheterodyne receiver.
T7A04: Selectivity is a receiver's ability to separate (discriminate between) signals on nearby frequencies, so you hear the one you want and reject the others.
T7A05: An oscillator generates a signal at a specific frequency. Every transmitter and receiver contains at least one.
T7A06: A transverter converts a transceiver's RF input and output to another band. For example, it can let an HF radio operate on a microwave band.
T7A07: PTT (Push-To-Talk) switches the transceiver from receive to transmit when the PTT line is grounded, which is what the button on your microphone does.
T7A08: Modulation is the process of combining information (such as speech) with an RF carrier so the information can be transmitted.
T7A09: Some VHF amplifiers have an SSB vs CW-FM switch. It sets the amplifier for proper operation in the selected mode: SSB needs linear amplification, while CW and FM can use more efficient non-linear settings. It doesn't change the transmitted mode itself.
T7A10: An RF power amplifier boosts the transceiver's output power. A potentiometer is a variable resistor and does not amplify.
T7A11: The VFO (Variable Frequency Oscillator) sets the operating frequency for receiving and transmitting. Turning the main tuning knob adjusts the VFO.
T7B01: Over-deviation means your FM signal is swinging too far in frequency, usually because your voice is too loud at the mic. Back away from the microphone or speak more softly.
T7B02: When a nearby broadcast radio picks up your ham signal, it's usually because the receiver can't reject strong signals outside its band (fundamental overload). The problem is in the receiver, not your transmitter.
T7B03: Fundamental overload (a strong signal overwhelming a receiver), harmonics (multiples of your frequency), and spurious emissions (unwanted signals) can all cause RF interference.
T7B04: Solid-state transmitters automatically reduce power when SWR is high to protect their output transistors. So high SWR can cause low output power. Low SWR is good.
T7B05: If a nearby receiver is overloaded by your signal, a filter at that receiver's antenna input that blocks your frequency is often the fix. A filter on your transmitter won't help if your signal itself is clean.
T7B06: First, make sure your own station is working properly. A good check is whether you interfere with your own radio or TV tuned to the same channel. If you don't, the problem is likely the neighbor's equipment.
T7B07: A band-reject (notch) filter can block the strong commercial FM broadcast signal (88-108 MHz) from reaching your 2-meter receiver. A preamplifier would make the overload worse.
T7B08: When a neighbor's device interferes with you, work with them cooperatively to find the device, politely let them know the FCC rules (Part 15 devices must not cause harmful interference), and make sure your own station is in order. All are appropriate.
T7B09: Most cable TV interference comes from loose or poorly installed connectors that let RF leak in. Check that all the TV coax connectors are properly installed before trying filters.
T7B10: Distorted audio through a repeater can come from being off frequency, talking too loudly or too close to the mic, or being in a poor location (weak or multipath signal). Any of them can be the cause.
T7B11: Distortion can be caused by RF feedback, where your own transmitted signal gets into the microphone cable. A clip-on ferrite choke on the cable blocks the RF and can eliminate the distortion.
T7C01: A dummy load is a resistor that absorbs your transmitter's power without radiating it. It lets you test your transmitter without putting a signal on the air and causing interference.
T7C02: An antenna analyzer measures SWR and impedance across a range of frequencies, showing where an antenna is resonant. A frequency counter only measures frequency.
T7C03: A typical dummy load is a 50-ohm non-inductive resistor on a heat sink. 50 ohms matches the transmitter, and the heat sink dissipates the power as heat.
T7C04: An SWR of 1:1 indicates a perfect match: no power is reflected back from the antenna. Higher ratios (such as 2:1 or 3:1) indicate greater mismatch.
T7C05: High SWR means reflected power returns to the transmitter, which can damage the output transistors. Solid-state radios reduce power automatically to protect them.
T7C06: A 4:1 SWR indicates a significant impedance mismatch between the feed line and the antenna. It's not a measure of gain or loss in dB.
T7C07: Power lost in a feed line is converted to heat. Higher-loss cable and higher frequencies mean more power wasted as heat.
T7C08: A directional wattmeter measures forward and reflected power, from which SWR can be calculated. Many SWR meters work the same way. (Iambic pentameter is poetry!)
T7C09: Moisture getting into coax is a common cause of failure. Water raises losses and corrodes the conductors. Seal outdoor connectors well.
T7C10: Sunlight's UV rays break down the plastic jacket over time, causing cracks that let water into the cable. UV-resistant jackets last much longer outdoors.
T7C11: Foam dielectric coax has less loss per foot than solid dielectric, because foam (mostly air) absorbs less energy. The tradeoff is that it's more prone to moisture problems.
T7D01: Electric potential (voltage) is measured with a voltmeter. An ammeter measures current, and an ohmmeter measures resistance.
T7D02: A voltmeter is connected in parallel with (across) the component, since voltage is the difference between two points.
T7D03: To measure current, the meter must be connected in series, so the current flows through it. You break the circuit and insert the meter.
T7D05: An ohmmeter applies a small known current from its internal battery and measures the resulting voltage, then calculates resistance (R = E / I).
T7D06: On the resistance setting, the meter supplies its own current and expects an unpowered circuit. Connecting it across a live voltage can damage the meter. Always check the switch position before measuring voltage.
T7D07: A multimeter measures voltage, resistance, and usually current. It does not measure signal strength, impedance, or reactance.
T7D08: Acid-core solder is for plumbing. The acid flux corrodes electronic components and circuit boards. Use rosin-core solder for electronics.
T7D09: A cold solder joint looks rough, lumpy, or grainy (dull) because the solder didn't melt and flow properly. A good joint is smooth and shiny.
T7D10: When an ohmmeter is connected to a discharged capacitor, the capacitor first draws current (low resistance) and then charges up, so the reading increases over time.
T7D11: Always make sure the circuit is unpowered before measuring resistance. Voltage in the circuit gives wrong readings and can damage the meter.
